My data

My fairness dataset is the Adult Income Dataset. One row is one person, with 5000 total rows. My sports dataset is the Marathon Race Results Dataset. One row is one runner, with 26598 total rows.

put_in_place("fairness.csv")
put_in_place("sports.csv")

fairness <- read_csv("data/fairness.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sports <- read_csv("data/sports.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

if (looks_damaged(fairness) || looks_damaged(sports)) {
  stop("One of your data files looks damaged (each row in one column): it ",
       "may have been re-saved by a spreadsheet app. Ask your instructor ",
       "for a fresh copy.", call. = FALSE)
}

# PART A · FAIRNESS ==========================================================

# A0 · See it update ---------------------------------------------------------
# A ready count plot of one of your Fairness columns. Nothing to code.

Part A · Fairness

A0 · See it update

a0_column <- pick_a_column(fairness)

a0 <- ggplot(fairness, aes(y = .data[[a0_column]])) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Dawson's first plot", x = "Count", y = a0_column)

show_plot(a0)

Yes, the updated title appeared in the report and slides.

A1 · Label it

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = education,
    has_outcome = income == ">50K"
  )

a1_base <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")

a1 <- a1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Income Above $50K by Education Level",
    subtitle = "Adult dataset (n = 5000)",
    x = "Share earning above/below",
    y = "Education level",
    fill = "Income above $50K"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)

show_plot(a1)

I changed the x-axis label the most because I wanted to make it clear that the percentages represent income categories within each education group. I think a reader could understand the plot without an explanation because the title, axes, and legend describe what is being compared.

A2 · Choose a scale

a2 <- fairness %>%
  filter(capital_gain > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = capital_gain)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Capital Gains",
    x = "Capital gain (dollars, log scale)",
    y = "Count"
  )

a2_reason <- "With linear scale, the graph would be skewed to the right, making
the values hard to see"

show_plot(a2)

I used a logarithmic scale for capital gain because most values are small, while some are much larger. Compared with a linear scale, the log scale makes the differences among smaller positive values easier to see. I excluded 4563 zero or negative values because they cannot be displayed on a logarithmic scale.

A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

# YOUR TURN 1: replace "replace me" with your second column (no quotes).
a3_rates <- a_data %>%
  mutate(panel = sex) %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = mean(has_outcome), .groups = "drop")

a3_fixed <- ggplot(a3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Income Above $50K by Education and Sex",
    x = "Education level",
    y = "Share earning above $50K"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, size = 8)
  )

a3_free <- a3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")

# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
# a3_fixed <- ggplot(a3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +

#   labs(title = "___", x = "___", y = "___ (%)")

# YOUR TURN 3: which one would you publish, "fixed" or "free_y"? Why?
a3_choice <- "fixed"
a3_reason <- "Fixed scales make it easier to compare the percentage earning
above $50K between sex categories because both panels use the same y-axis."

show_plot(a3_fixed)
show_plot(a3_free)

I chose fixed scales because they make it easier to compare income percentages between the panels. The reader gains a consistent scale for comparison, but smaller differences within a panel may be harder to see than with free scales. The percentages vary across education levels and between the sex categories. The smallest education-by-sex group, which is preschool-female, has only one observation, so its percentage should be interpreted cautiously.

A4 · Compared to what?

a4_clouds <- a_data %>%
  filter(education %in% c("Bachelors", "HS-grad")) %>%
  make_clouds(education, capital_gain)
# YOUR TURN 1: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___: the column
# with your groups, two of its values, and your numeric column.
# a4_clouds <- a_data %>%
#   filter(___ %in% c("___", "___")) %>%
#   make_clouds(___, ___)

a4 <- ggplot(a4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(
    title = "Capital Gains: Bachelors vs. High School Graduates",
    x = "Education level",
    y = "Capital gain (dollars)"
  )
# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
# a4 <- ggplot(a4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
#   geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
#   facet_wrap(~ kind) +
#   labs(title = "___", x = "___", y = "___ (units)")

show_plot(a4)

The individual values show considerable overlap between the two education groups, with many people having little or no capital gain. The resampled means show how much the average could vary between samples. Comparing the panels helps distinguish differences between individual people from differences between group averages.

A5 · Color for every reader

a5 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = education, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Education Levels by Sex",
    x = "Count",
    y = "Education level",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

show_plot(a5)

# See it: your plot as a reader with red-green color blindness might see it.
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(a5)
2 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;
the blue-yellow one is an approximation.
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  view                      smallest_difference at_least_20
  <chr>                                   <dbl> <chr>      
1 Red-green (deuteranopia)                 99.5 Yes        
2 Red-green (protanopia)                  119.  Yes        
3 Blue-yellow (approximate)                81.3 Yes        
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Blue-yellow (approximate)"))

I used the sex column for color because it has only a few categories, making the colors easier to distinguish. I chose a viridis color scale to improve accessibility for readers with color-vision differences. I also separated the categories into panels so readers do not have to rely on color alone. In the simulated views, the categories can still be identified using the panel labels.

Part B · Sports

B1 · Label it

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = age_group,
    has_outcome = place_overall <= 100,
    value = finish_net_minutes
  )

b1_base <- ggplot(b_data, aes(x = age_group, y = finish_net_minutes)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = gender), width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.3)

b1 <- b1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Finishing Time by Age Group and Gender",
    subtitle = "Comparison of runners' finishing times across age groups",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Net finishing time (minutes)",
    color = "Gender"
  )

show_plot(b1)

The plot shows how runners’ finishing times vary across age groups and gender categories. I think the y-axis label is the most helpful because it explains that finishing times are measured in minutes.

B2 · Choose a scale

b2 <- b_data %>%
  filter(place_overall > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = place_overall)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Overall Finishing Positions",
    x = "Overall finishing position (log scale)",
    y = "Count"
  )

b2_reason <- "With a linear scale, basically everything is at the same level and
the points where it actually changes get smushed and aren't readable data."

show_plot(b2)

I used a logarithmic scale for overall finishing position to display a wide range of ranks. This spreads out the lower ranks and compresses the higher ranks, making the earlier finishing positions easier to distinguish. No zero or negative finishing positions were removed.

B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

b3_data <- b_data %>%
  drop_na(gender, age_group, finish_net_minutes) %>%
  add_count(gender, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(
    panel = paste0(gender, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")
  )

b3_fixed <- ggplot(
  b3_data,
  aes(x = age_group, y = finish_net_minutes)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  labs(
    title = "Finishing Times by Age Group and Gender",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Net finishing time (minutes)"
  )

b3_free <- b3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")

b3_choice <- "fixed"

b3_reason <- "A fixed scale makes it much easier to compare the finishing times
across gender groups."

show_plot(b3_fixed)
show_plot(b3_free)

I chose fixed scales because they allow finishing times to be compared directly between the gender panels. The reader gains a consistent y-axis, although differences within each panel may be less noticeable than with free scales. The boxplots show how finishing times vary across age groups and gender categories. The smaller panel contains 11423 runners, which is important to consider when comparing the groups.

B4 · Compared to what?

b4_clouds <- b_data %>%
  filter(gender %in% c("M", "W")) %>%
  make_clouds(gender, finish_net_minutes)

b4 <- ggplot(b4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(
    title = "Finishing Times by Gender",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Net finishing time (minutes)"
  )

show_plot(b4)

The individual finishing times show variation within both gender groups, with runners from both groups having overlapping finishing times. The resampled means show how much the average finishing time could vary between samples. This helps distinguish differences between individual runners from differences between the group averages.

B5 · Color for every reader

b5 <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = gender, fill = gender)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Boston Marathon Runners by Gender",
    x = "Number of runners",
    y = "Gender",
    fill = "Gender"
  )

show_plot(b5)

show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(b5)
2 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;
the blue-yellow one is an approximation.

  view                      smallest_difference at_least_20
  <chr>                                   <dbl> <chr>      
1 Red-green (deuteranopia)                 99.5 Yes        
2 Red-green (protanopia)                  119.  Yes        
3 Blue-yellow (approximate)                81.3 Yes        
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Blue-yellow (approximate)"))

I used gender for the fill colors because it has only a few categories, making the colors easier to distinguish. I chose the viridis color scale to improve accessibility for readers with color-vision differences. I also put gender on the y-axis so readers can identify the categories without relying only on color. The categories remain identifiable in the simulated views because of the axis labels.

One thing I tried in my slides, and why

I focused my slides on income differences across education levels and sex categories. I used the fixed-scale version of my A3 plot so readers could compare percentages between the panels without having to account for different axis ranges. I also organized the slides so the research question comes before the main finding and the limitations come afterward.
